title: Truth tables, tautologies, and contraposition
section: Logic ▷ Logical Equivalences and Truth Tables
terms: truth table; logical equivalence; tautology; contradiction; contrapositive; converse; inverse of an implication; De Morgan laws; distributive laws; excluded middle; quantifier negation.

exposition.text:
Two formulas are logically equivalent if they agree on every truth assignment. A tautology is
always true and a contradiction always false. The law of excluded middle is the tautology P ∨ ¬P .
De Morgan’s laws are ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q. Distributivity holds in
both directions between conjunction and disjunction.
The implication P ⇒ Q is equivalent to its contrapositive ¬Q ⇒ ¬P, but not generally to its
converse Q ⇒ P or inverse ¬P ⇒ ¬Q. The source labels contraposition as contradiction; these
are different notions. A useful extension for mathematical statements is quantifier negation:
¬∀x P(x) means ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) means ∀x ¬P(x).
A truth table lists every assignment of truth values to the variables and evaluates the formula
on each row. Double negation gives ¬¬P ≡ P . Conjunction and disjunction are each commu-
tative and associative. The distributive identities are P ∧ (Q ∨ R) ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R) and
P ∨(Q ∧R) ≡ (P ∨ Q) ∧(P ∨R). These identities justify algebraic simplification without checking
every row separately.

question.text:
Assume P ⇒ Q, Q ⇒ R, and ¬P ⇒ ¬R. Which must hold?
(A) P, Q, R are all true
(B) P, Q, R are all false
(C) P, Q, R have the same truth value
(D) P and R have opposite truth values
(E) Q is true

solution.text:
The last implication has contrapositive R ⇒ P . Together these give the cycle P ⇒ Q ⇒
R ⇒ P . Thus if any is true all are true, and otherwise all are false.

question.text:
What is the negation of ∀x ∈ R ∃y ∈ R (y > x and f(y) > 0)?
(A) ∀x ∀y (y ≤ x or f (y) ≤ 0)
(B) ∃x ∀y (y ≤ x or f (y) ≤ 0)
(C) ∃x ∃y (y ≤ x and f(y) ≤ 0)
(D) ∀x ∃y (y ≤ x and f(y) ≤ 0)
(E) ∃x ∀y (y > x and f(y) ≤ 0)

solution.text:
Reverse each quantifier and negate the final conjunction. The result is that some real x has
no larger y with positive f (y), equivalently ∃x∀y [y ≤ x ∨ f (y) ≤ 0].

question.text:
The implication P ⇒ Q is true, but its converse and inverse are both false. Which truth assign-
ment is possible?
(A) P = T, Q = T
(B) P = T, Q = F
(C) P = F, Q = T
(D) P = F, Q = F
(E) No such assignment exists.

solution.text:
The converse Q ⇒ P is false exactly at Q = T, P = F. At that assignment the original
implication is vacuously true and the inverse ¬P ⇒ ¬Q is false. Converse and inverse are
equivalent to each other, but not to the original implication.

question.text:
Which is logically equivalent to (P ∨ Q) ⇒ R?
(A) R ⇒ (P ∨ Q) (B) P ∧ Q ∧ R
(C) (P ∧ Q) ⇒ R (D) (P ⇒ R) ∨ (Q ⇒ R)
(E) (P ⇒ R) ∧ (Q ⇒ R)

solution.text:
The implication equals (¬P ∧ ¬Q) ∨ R. Distributing gives (¬P ∨ R) ∧ (¬Q ∨ R), which is the
conjunction of the two implications.

question.text:
Classify F = (P ⇒ Q) ∧ P ∧ ¬Q and G = P ∨ ¬P .
(A) Both are tautologies.
(B) Both are contradictions.
(C) F is a tautology and G a contradiction.
(D) F is a contradiction and G a tautology.
(E) Both are true for some assignments and false for others.

solution.text:
If P and ¬Q are true, the implication in F is false; otherwise another conjunct is false.
Thus F is always false. One of P, ¬P is always true, so G is always true. The formula F is
a contradiction; this is distinct from replacing an implication by its contrapositive.

question.text:
Which formula is equivalent to ¬¬P ∧ (Q ∨ (R ∨ Q))?
(A) (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R) (B) (P ∨ Q) ∧ (P ∨ R)
(C) P ∨ (Q ∧ R) (D) (P ∧ Q) ∨ R
(E) P ∧ Q ∧ R

solution.text:
Double negation removes the two negations. Associativity and commutativity collect the
repeated Q; Q ∨ Q ≡ Q. Distributing P ∧ (Q ∨ R) then gives the stated expression. For
example, choice D incorrectly allows R to make the formula true when P is false.
